To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the BLV TM trimer-of-hairs structure reveals the presence of a charge-surrounded pocket on the central coil and that electrostatic interactions with basic residues are critical to membrane fusibility and (ii) the presence of a group of aspartate residues that is strikingly similar among divergent viruses promotes assembly of the trims-of-hairs through interactions with a small chloride ion.

the membrane-proximal region of the class-1 viral fusion protein is stabilized by electrostatic interactions with chloride ions and that the central coiled-coil is stabilized by charge-surrounded pockets that are targeted by small peptides.
The bovine leukaemic virus transmembrane (TM) glycoprotein is the only retroviral TM glycoprotein structure available.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanism of viral membrane fusion and the development of small-molecule inhibitors of this process.
the molecular basis of retroviral entry into cells and the development of small molecule inhibitors of this process.
understanding the structure, function and assembly of retroviral fusion proteins.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the structure of bovine leukemia virus transmembrane (TM) glycoprotein reveals a group of conserved asparagine residues and a charge-surrounded pocket on the coiled coil that play key roles in viral membrane fusion.
this study reveals a group of conserved asparagine residues in the trimer-of-α-hairpins of retroviral class-1 fusion glycoproteins.
the charge-surrounded pockets and the electrostatic interactions with the basic residues that cluster round the pocket are critical to the membrane fusion of the BLV TM protein.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified the molecular mechanism by which a class-1 fusion protein assembles into a fusogenic structure.
the BLV TM protein structure provides new insights into membrane fusion and viral pathogenesis.

electrostatic interactions with chloride ions and basic residues that cluster in a hydrophobic pocket are critical to the function of class-1 viral fusion proteins and are potential targets for the design of small-molecule therapeutics.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the electrostatics and charge-surrounded hydrophilic pockets of class-1 fusion protein trimers are critical to their function and that these features are common to many viruses.
the electrostatic interactions between small ions and conserved residues at the membrane distal end of the class-1 fusion protein trimer-of-hairs are critical to membrane fusogenic activity.
small molecules that interact with charge-surrounded pockets and small ions should be effective inhibitors of viral fusion proteins.
